summary: RFC 3263 defines how a SIP implementation locates the next-hop server for a URI using DNS. As networks move from IPv4-only to dual-stack, users need a good experience. This proposed standard updates the procedure to locate servers in dual-stack networks, for example by trying both address families in a sensible way.

plainLanguage.summary: When you have both an old and a new road to a friend's house, you should try both and not get stuck on a broken one. This tells phone software how to do that.

questions: how do sip clients locate servers in a dual stack network
why can sip not race ipv4 and ipv6 like http
how are sip srv records ordered with ipv6 addresses
subtitle: How a SIP client that speaks both IPv4 and IPv6 should look up and order the addresses of a server.

tldr.problem: RFC 3263 tells SIP clients to look up an A or AAAA record, which works poorly for dual-stack clients and can add connection delay.
tldr.mechanism: A dual-stack client SHOULD look up address records for every address family it supports and put all the results in one list. A server can use SRV priorities to signal a preferred family, and address ordering within one SRV target follows RFC 6724.
tldr.outcome: It prepares the ground for applying Happy Eyeballs to SIP and clarifies how SRV ordering and address selection fit together. It updates RFC 3263.

facts.label: Address lookup rule
facts.value: SHOULD look up all supported families

today: RFC 7984 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2016. It updates RFC 3263 and, according to the metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC.

sections.title: Why SIP Needs Dual-Stack Rules
sections.content:
SIP supports both IPv4 and IPv6, but the RFC says that support does not fully cover the mixed environments of the transition from IPv4 to IPv6. A dual-stack host will likely suffer greater connection delay, and a worse user experience, than an IPv4-only host. The Happy Eyeballs algorithm (RFC 6555) was developed to fix that for other protocols.

This document updates the DNS lookup procedures of RFC 3263 in preparation for a later specification of Happy Eyeballs for SIP. How a client then picks the best way to set up a network flow is out of scope here.
sections.plainLanguage: Computers now have an old kind of address and a new kind. When a computer knows both, it can get slow if it tries them badly. This RFC sets up the first step to fix that.

sections.title: Terms and Scope of Dual-Stack
sections.content:
The document uses SIP server to mean a user agent server, registrar, redirect server, a SIP proxy acting as a user agent server, or a B2BUA acting as a user agent server. Address records means the DNS records that map a name to addresses in the families the entity supports, such as A records for IPv4 and AAAA records for IPv6, whether or not the family existed when the document was approved.

The term dual-stack is used broadly. It covers any client with access to several communication methods that have distinct addressing characteristics, such as a device with multiple interfaces, or address families created in the future.
sections.plainLanguage: A 'dual-stack' computer is like a person who speaks two languages. The RFC says the same ideas also work for more than two.

sections.title: Looking Up Every Address Family
sections.content:
RFC 3263 says that when the target is not a numeric IP address and a port is given, or when no SRV records are found, the client performs an A or AAAA lookup. RFC 6555 documents that this is not effective for dual-stack clients and can add significant connection delay.

So the RFC adds a normative rule: the dual-stack client SHOULD look up address records for all address families it supports for the domain name and add the resulting addresses to the list to be contacted. A client MUST be prepared for records in families it does not support, and such records MUST be ignored as unusable.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of asking for just one kind of address, ask for all the kinds you understand and put them in one list. Ignore any kind you cannot use.

sections.title: Signalling a Preferred Address Family
sections.content:
Happy Eyeballs works well for HTTP because a client can open one TCP connection over IPv4 and one over IPv6 and keep whichever finishes first. Opening a connection does not change the server's state, so the client sends the request on only one of them.

SIP cannot usually do this. If requests go out as single UDP packets, sending two copies to two addresses risks two copies of the request travelling through the SIP network at once. The sender cannot test a route in a way that does not change state. A destination that receives the second copy SHOULD reject it with response code 482, but the RFC notes that this is not enough to prevent user-visible differences, because an upstream proxy may fork the second request onwards, for example to voicemail.

Instead, a service may use DNS SRV records to show a preference. A server with a high-latency or low-capacity IPv4 tunnel can publish IPv6-only host names at the lowest SRV priority and host names resolving in both families at the next priority. Such single-family host names are discouraged by RFC 6555 and SHOULD be used only as targets of SRV records for an aggregate host name that ultimately resolves in all families the client supports.
sections.plainLanguage: Knocking on two doors at once could make two people answer a call meant for one. So instead, a house can put a sign saying 'please use the new door first'.

sections.title: SRV Order and RFC 6724 Address Order
sections.content:
RFC 6157 says the addresses for a single target name must be contacted in the order given by the address selection algorithms of RFC 6724. This RFC clarifies the scope: the set of addresses given to one run of destination address selection MUST be the address records for the target name in a single SRV record (or the URI name or NAPTR-derived name if there are no SRV records). The algorithm MUST NOT reorder addresses derived from different SRV records.

The result is two levels of ordering. The major order comes from the SRV priority and weight fields (RFC 2782). The minor order, among addresses from one SRV target, comes from RFC 6724, typically through the getaddrinfo() function.
sections.plainLanguage: First you sort the shops by the list you were given. Then, inside each shop, you sort the doors. You never mix doors from different shops.

sections.title: A Worked Ordering Example
sections.content:
The RFC takes example.com with TCP and two SRV records: sip-1.example.com at priority 10 and sip-2.example.com at priority 20, both on port 5060. Each target has three AAAA and three A records, already ordered by RFC 6724 with IPv6 first.

The complete list is the three IPv6 and three IPv4 addresses of sip-1, followed by the three IPv6 and three IPv4 addresses of sip-2. The addresses of the two targets are not interleaved, and the RFC says this would hold even if the SRV records had the same priority and were randomly ordered by weight.
sections.plainLanguage: All of the first shop's doors come first, then all of the second shop's doors, even if the second shop has a fancier new door.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says its two new procedures introduce no new security considerations. A client may contact additional target addresses, or contact them in a different order than RFC 3263 prescribes, but it has always been assumed that a client wanting to send to a URI may contact any target listed in DNS.

The specific attacks and threat models of SIP, DNS, SRV records and Happy Eyeballs are left to their own specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC says it only changes which listed addresses you try and in what order, so it does not open any new door for bad guys.

layers.label: SRV records
layers.detail: Priority and weight (RFC 2782) order the target names

layers.label: Address records of one target
layers.detail: RFC 6724 orders the A and AAAA addresses

layers.label: Final contact list
layers.detail: Addresses of different SRV targets are never interleaved
